claims.text: A machine-learning model combining binary-phase-diagram descriptors, ab initio defect-scattering data, and finite-temperature corrections can predict the electrical conductivity of bulk HfNbTaTiZr.
The model will capture oxygen-defect effects across 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
The proposed model will outperform analytical models based on ideal, defect-free crystals.
Bulk HfNbTaTiZr is a disordered BCC or near-BCC solid solution with intrinsic lattice distortions.
The modeled HfNbTaTiZr contains approximately 1 wt.% oxygen.
Binary-alloy or binary-phase-diagram features can be transformed into expandable features applicable to multielement alloys.
Binary-phase-diagram-inspired machine learning can improve HEA phase prediction relative to other statistical phase-prediction approaches.
Oxygen occupies interstitial defect sites in the alloy.
Oxygen defects and local lattice distortions perturb the electronic structure and carrier-scattering rates.
Impurity-driven scattering dominates the electrical conductivity of 1 wt.% oxygen HfNbTaTiZr from 0 to 200 K.
Phonon scattering and defect–phonon interactions dominate conductivity from 300 to 1200 K.
Integrating experimentally informed descriptors and ab initio defect-scattering data allows the model to adjust electronic-band and carrier-scattering predictions for a defect-laden microstructure.
Representing both low-temperature impurity scattering and high-temperature phonon/defect–phonon scattering improves conductivity-prediction accuracy.
The proposed model will improve conductivity-prediction accuracy by approximately 10–20% relative to perfect-crystal models.
Oxygen impurity scattering will produce relatively lower conductivity in the 0–200 K regime.
High-temperature conductivity will be modulated by phonons and defect interactions.
Traditional analytical conductivity models omit temperature-dependent defect scattering and impurity effects.
The proposed applicability domain is HfNbTaTiZr near 1 wt.% oxygen over 0–200 K and 300–1200 K.
Validity outside the stated temperature intervals or at other oxygen concentrations is unestablished.
Deviation greater than approximately 20% across both temperature regimes, or failure to reproduce the stipulated temperature-dependent behavior, would falsify the hypothesis.
